MS NOW host Chris Hayes on Monday noted it’s been less than a week since Republicans lost the House and Senate to Democrats, exclaiming in amazement, “And already, [President Donald] Trump is back with his half-assed attempt to spin the big lie yet again.”

Trump on Monday indeed attempted to revive “the big lie” around his 2020 election defeat by former President Joe Biden in suggesting the midterms were rigged against him, despite occasional comments in recent days about wanting to work with the triumphant Democrats.

“Trump asked on social media, quote, ‘Does anybody really believe that this “Election” was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???’” Hayes explained. “‘Some early voting “dumps” were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote.’”

Hayes argued, “Sounds a lot like 2020, doesn’t it? Remember, a lot of dump talk back then?”

He went on to note that Trump’s midterms denial was “promptly smacked down” by once-leading members of his own movement, however, including conservative pundit Megyn Kelly, former Trump aide Steve Bannon and former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.).

Hayes brought on political consultant and Bulwark publisher Sarah Longwell to ask what this might mean, as Trump received vast support from his base in 2020 in denying the election, and asked her if “the big lie” is going anywhere this time — like it dangerously did in 2021.

“It’s not going anywhere,” Longwell told Hayes. “Not this time. And look, I think it’s hard for people to confidently say that, because we’ve seen Trump pull weird rabbits out of his hat on things like this, but I gotta tell ya, this is a guy with a 35% approval rating overall.”

She added, “And every piece of data, not just the vote count, not just the fact that they lost in Mississippi and Kansas and South Carolina, but also anybody who is doing focus groups, anybody who’s doing polling, you can see the data everywhere, about how upset voters are.”

Longwell noted this widespread frustration — about the U.S. economy, Trump’s ongoing war on Iran, his alleged corruption and obsession with data centers — clearly won out at the polls last week despite Trump’s baseless suggestion that he was once again cheated.

Trump notably made the midterms all about himself despite disastrous approval ratings amid a nationwide affordability crisis he dismissed and exacerbated with his unpopular war, leading to a Democratic sweep and an opening for potential congressional investigations.

Longwell argued Trump is now “so weak” — and practically incapable of leading his party.

“Part of what you’re seeing in the pushback is that Trump is now a weak, lame-duck president,” she said. “Nobody’s trying to curry favor with him. Nobody’s trying to relitigate this election. These Republicans now are going to use this as an opportunity.”

Longwell explained, “To say, ‘Trump is done, we need to move forward with something else.’ And they’re going to start pitching their ideas for what that is. No one’s going to go along with this, this time — except some real braindead, dead-ender types.”
